newsitem.title: USA: Kevorkian supporters applaud Supreme Court decision.
newsitem.headline: Kevorkian supporters applaud Supreme Court decision.

text.p: Advocates on both sides of the assisted-suicide debate in Dr. Jack Kevorkian's home state applauded Tuesday the Supreme Court's decision to hear arguments on the controversial practice.
But Geoffrey Fieger, attorney for the country's best-known assisted-suicide crusader, does not think the nation's high court will rule in favour of the right-to-die-movement.
Fieger told reporters Tuesday he is concerned that conservative members of the nation's high court may use the opportunity to thwart Kevorkian's efforts.
"It would have been better if the Supreme Court did not hear this issue," said Fieger.

Opening the way for a landmark decision, the high court said Tuesday it will review laws in New York and Washington states that ban a mentally competent, terminally ill person from dying with a doctor's help.

The cases do not involve Kevorkian. The retired pathologist, who lives in the Detroit suburb of West Bloomfield, has fanned the debate on a national scale by helping at least 41 people from across the country die since 1990.
Janet Good, founder of the Hemlock Society of Michigan, a right-to-die advocacy group, said she is glad the Supreme Court has finally decided to take up the issue.
"It's about time. The people of this country in all the polls have said what they want, and I'm confident the Supreme Court will follow the lower courts," said Good.
Good, who has been at Kevorkian's side when he helped people die and is herself terminally ill with pancreatic cancer, said she is also happy that Kevorkian is not involved in the cases.
"This is an issue that goes beyond Kevorkian," she said.

Kevorkian's arch rival, Oakland County, Michigan, Prosecutor Richard Thompson, said he welcomed the Supreme Court's decision. He expressed confidence the court will find there is no constitutional right for doctor-assisted suicide.
"It would drastically transform the physician-patient relationship, and change the medical profession from healers into killers," Thompson said in a statement.

Thompson lost his primary bid for re-election last month, partly because of his two unsuccessful attempts to put Kevorkian behind bars. A total of three juries have acquitted Kevorkian on assisted-suicide charges relating to five deaths.
American Medical Association Chair Dr. Nancy Dickey said in a statement she is pleased the Supreme Court will make a declaration on what she called a "misguided and unethical practice."
Another Kevorkian foe, Cardinal Adam Maida, Archbishop of Detroit, said he is concerned about what the court may rule.
"Our experience with Supreme Court rulings has shown us that the moral values of life and death are often ignored in the debate over legal precedents," he said in a statement.

Diane Trombley, a spokeswoman for Right To Life-Lifespan of Metro Detroit, predicted the court's ruling will not settle the matter. She noted the controversy that still rages more than 20 years after the decision legalising abortion.
